extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and historians
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of how a sovereign or commonwealth should provide for public defence across different stages of societal development; compares militias and standing armies, their costs, and their relative effectiveness with historical examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: First duty of the sovereign: protection by military force
rubrics_metrics.description: The first duty of the sovereign, that of protecting the society from the violence and invasion of other independent societies, can be performed only by means of a military force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This establishes defence as a primary sovereign obligation and frames subsequent discussion of how that obligation imposes expense and institutional requirements. The passage uses this as the normative starting point for evaluating forms of military provision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defense expense varies with the state of society
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense both of preparing this military force in time of peace, and of employing it in time of war, is very different in the different states of society, in the different periods of improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides assessment of defence policy by requiring attention to social structure and economic development (hunters, shepherds, husbandmen, artificers/manufacturers). Examples throughout text illustrate how the same defence duty produces different fiscal burdens depending on societal organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hunter societies: self-maintained warriors, negligible public expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Among nations of hunters... every man is a warrior, as well as a hunter... His society is at no sort of expense, either to prepare him for the field, or to maintain him while he is in it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criterion: where ordinary life already trains and sustains warriors, public expenditure for defence preparation and maintenance is minimal. Implication: small, irregular forces; limited capacity for sustained large-scale warfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shepherd societies: mobile self-sustaining armies, low sovereign expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Among nations of shepherds... every man is, in the same manner, a warrior... When he takes the field... he is maintained by his own herds and flocks... His chief or sovereign is at no sort of expense in preparing him for the field; and when he is in it, the chance of plunder is the only pay which he either expects or requires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion highlights mobility and potential for very large armies in pastoral societies; sovereign fiscal burden remains low because troops bring their own subsistence. Examples: Tartars, Arabs; but also notes limits (household left vulnerable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Husbandmen/agricultural settlements: partial public expense and seasonal levies
rubrics_metrics.description: Among those nations of husbandmen who have little foreign commerce... every man either is a warrior, or easily becomes such... it seldom costs the sovereign or commonwealth any expense to prepare them for the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment must consider fixed habitation and agricultural seasonality: only a portion of the population serves, and campaigns timed after seedtime and before harvest reduce economic cost. Sovereign expense still limited compared to industrial societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactures and complex art of war necessitate public maintenance
rubrics_metrics.description: In a more advanced state of society, two different causes contribute to render it altogether impossible that they who take the field should maintain themselves at their own expense. Those two causes are, the progress of manufactures, and the improvement in the art of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many citizens are artificers/manufacturers (no independent subsistence) and war becomes prolonged/complicated, the state must maintain soldiers; criterion for transitioning to public pay and standing forces. Examples: artisans cannot leave their work without losing livelihood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two institutional methods of provision: militia vs standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: The state may either... by means of a very rigorous police ... enforce the practice of military exercises (militia), or... by maintaining and employing a certain number of citizens in the constant practice of military exercises, it may render the trade of a soldier a particular trade (standing army).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a categorical evaluative distinction: choice between compulsory/periodic citizen training and a professional permanent force. Each method has distinct fiscal, social, and military trade-offs discussed at length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and hallmarks of a standing army
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of military exercises is the sole or principal occupation of the soldiers of a standing army, and the maintenance or pay which the state affords them is the principal and ordinary fund of their subsistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides evaluation toward attributes such as daily exercise, professionalization, higher discipline, prompt obedience, and greater effectiveness in modern war; historical examples (Philip of Macedon, Roman standing armies) illustrate superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and limitations of a militia
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of military exercises is only the occasional occupation of the soldiers of a militia, and they derive the principal and ordinary fund of their subsistence from some other occupation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Militias are evaluated by frequency of exercise, attachment/regimentation, and competing civilian duties. The text notes militias are inferior in discipline and readiness, though regimented militias (e.g., England, Switzerland) vary in quality. Militias attached to traditional chiefs may approach standing-army obedience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern warfare values regularity, order, and prompt obedience over individual dexterity
rubrics_metrics.description: Regularity, order, and prompt obedience to command, are qualities which, in modern armies, are of more importance towards determining the fate of battles, than the dexterity and skill of the soldiers in the use of their arms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because firearms introduce noise, smoke, and invisible danger, mass discipline and obedience become decisive. This criterion favors forces with daily collective training (standing armies) over infrequent-exercise militias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of exercise as a determinant of military competence
rubrics_metrics.description: The soldiers who are exercised only once a week, or once a-month, can never be so expert... as those who are exercised every day, or every other day; ... in what is called discipline, or in the habit of ready obedience, a militia must always be much inferior to a well disciplined and well exercised standing army.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: assess training cadence when judging troop quality. Examples include Prussian troops' superiority attributed to more frequent exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Militias can transform into standing armies after repeated campaigns
rubrics_metrics.description: A militia of any kind... which has served for several successive campaigns in the field, becomes in every respect a standing army. The soldiers are every day exercised in the use of their arms, and... habituated to the same prompt obedience which takes place in standing armies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Temporal/durational criterion: the operational tempo and accumulated service can convert militia forces into de facto professional forces; example applied to American militia in prolonged conflict.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability constraint: proportion of soldiers to inhabitants
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the civilized nations of modern Europe, it is commonly computed, that not more than the one hundredth part of the inhabitants of any country can be employed as soldiers, without ruin to the country which pays the expense of their service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiscal/economic constraint for policy: when evaluating army size, consider maximum sustainable ratio of soldiers to population to avoid economic ruin.

rubrics_metrics.name: State responsibility for institutionalized training and preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of preparing the army for the field seems not to have become considerable in any nation, till long after that of maintaining it in the field had devolved entirely upon the sovereign or commonwealth... In all the different republics of ancient Greece, to learn his military exercises, was a necessary part of education imposed by the state upon every free citizen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion: successful standing forces require state institutions (public fields, gymnasia, ordinances for archery practice). Evaluators/policymakers should consider whether the state builds and funds training infrastructure rather than relying solely on ad hoc measures.
